data.content_ref: inline:The target's defense against induction is self-defeating because it justifies preference not only via verisimilitude (already challenged) but via the forward-looking claim that the better-corroborated theory 'offers the best chance for learning through falsification' and that the methodological rule is chosen 'to maximize potential knowledge growth.' These are projections from a theory's past test-performance to its future epistemic productivity. Claiming that a theory which has withstood severe tests so far will provide the best future learning opportunities requires assuming that past severity is relevant to future learning conditions—an inductive assumption about continuity. The target cannot simultaneously reject inductive inference as illegitimate for truth/survival projections while invoking it for learning/growth projections. The 'methodological rule vs. inductive principle' distinction thus collapses for the pragmatic branch of the target's own argument, satisfying countercondition 3 from a novel angle: the learning-justification is functionally an inductive principle dressed as a rule.
